mcq.q: Which statement about a cheque is correct under Section 6?
options: It can be drawn on any person
It is a bill of exchange addressed to a named bank, payable only on demand
It can be made payable three months after date
It must be accepted by the bank before payment
mcq.explain: Under Section 6, a cheque is a bill of exchange addressed to a named bank and payable only on demand. Both an electronic cheque and the scanned image of a truncated paper cheque fall within this definition. A cheque does not need acceptance; the bank pays it on presentment if funds are available.
mcq.fast: Cheque = bill + drawn on a banker + on demand only.

mcq.q: Which of these is a valid promissory note?
options: "I promise to pay Rohan ₹10,000 seven days after the death of Sohan."
"I promise to pay Rohan ₹10,000 when I marry Priya."
"I promise to pay Rohan ₹10,000 if I pass the CA exam."
"I promise to pay Rohan ₹10,000 and all other sums due to him."
mcq.explain: A promissory note under Section 4 needs an unconditional undertaking to pay a certain sum. Payment after a person's death is certain to happen, though the time is uncertain, so it is valid. Payment on marriage or passing an exam is conditional, and "all other sums due" makes the amount uncertain.
mcq.fast: Death = certain event (valid). Marriage / passing / "other sums" = condition or uncertainty (invalid).

mcq.q: Because of Section 31 of the RBI Act, no private person may issue a promissory note payable to:
options: Bearer
A named person
The order of a named person
A named person or his order
mcq.explain: Section 31 of the RBI Act reserves bearer-on-demand paper to the RBI (and, where authorised, the Central Government); in particular no private person may issue a promissory note payable to bearer. Otherwise private bearer notes would act like currency.
mcq.fast: Bearer notes = currency = RBI's monopoly.

mcq.q: The parties to a bill of exchange are:
options: Maker and payee only
Banker and customer only
Drawer, drawee and payee
Promisor and promisee
mcq.explain: A bill of exchange under Section 5 is an order by the drawer directing the drawee to pay a certain sum to a certain person, the payee, or to his order or to bearer. A promissory note has only two original parties — the maker and the payee. In a cheque the drawee is always a banker.
mcq.fast: Bill = order = three parties. Note = promise = two parties.

mcq.q: A person who obtains a negotiable instrument for consideration, before maturity, without sufficient cause to believe that the transferor's title is defective, is a:
options: Holder only
Drawee in case of need
Indorser
Holder in due course — Section 9
mcq.explain: Section 9 defines a holder in due course as a person who, for consideration, became the possessor (bearer instrument) or payee or indorsee (order instrument) before maturity, without sufficient cause to believe that any defect existed in the title of the person from whom he derived his title. He gets a title free from defects.
mcq.topic: Meaning and characteristics of negotiable instruments (Section 13)
mcq.fast: Holder in due course = value + before maturity + good faith.

mcq.q: Sunil wants to transfer a cheque made out to "Sunil or order" to Tara. What must he do?
options: Simply hand it over
Indorse it and deliver it to Tara — Section 48
Get it registered with the bank
Assign it orally
mcq.explain: Under Section 48, an order instrument passes to a new holder only when it is indorsed and then delivered. Under Section 47 an instrument payable to bearer is negotiable by delivery alone. Without indorsement, the transferee of an order instrument does not become a holder.
mcq.fast: Bearer = deliver; Order = indorse + deliver.

mcq.q: A cheque of ₹1,50,000 is dishonoured for insufficiency of funds, and the drawer is convicted under Section 138. The maximum fine the court can impose is:
mcq.explain: Section 138 punishes a cheque bounced for want of funds with jail for up to two years, a fine of up to double the cheque value, or both. Twice ₹1,50,000 is ₹3,00,000. These limits apply when the other conditions — presentment, notice and non-payment — are met.
mcq.topic: Dishonour of cheques for insufficiency of funds (Sections 138 to 140)
mcq.fast: Fine ceiling = 2 × cheque amount; jail up to 2 years.

mcq.q: After a cheque bounces, the payee must send a written notice demanding payment within:
options: 15 days of the date of the cheque
3 months of receiving the return memo
30 days of receiving information of the dishonour from the bank
7 days of dishonour
mcq.explain: Under clause (b) of the proviso to Section 138, the payee or holder in due course must make a demand for payment by a written notice to the drawer within 30 days of receiving information from the bank about the return of the cheque as unpaid. The drawer then has 15 days from receipt of the notice to pay.
mcq.topic: Dishonour of cheques for insufficiency of funds (Sections 138 to 140)
mcq.fast: Bounce chain: present within validity -> notice within 30 days -> drawer pays within 15 days.

mcq.q: After receiving a valid demand notice, the drawer of a dishonoured cheque gets how many days to pay before an offence under Section 138 is complete?
options: 30 days
7 days
45 days
15 days
mcq.explain: Under clause (c) of the proviso to Section 138, the drawer commits the offence only if he does not pay within 15 days after the notice reaches him. The cause of action arises after these 15 days expire, and the complaint must then be filed within one month under Section 142.
mcq.topic: Dishonour of cheques for insufficiency of funds (Sections 138 to 140)
mcq.fast: 30 days for the notice, 15 days for the drawer to pay, 1 month to file.

mcq.q: A complaint for an offence under Section 138 must be filed within:
options: One month of the date on which the cause of action arises — Section 142
Six months of dishonour
One year of the cheque date
Fifteen days of the notice
mcq.explain: Section 142 requires the complaint to be made in writing by the payee or holder in due course within one month of the date on which the cause of action arises, that is, after the 15-day period for payment expires. The court may take cognizance of a later complaint if the complainant shows sufficient cause for the delay.
mcq.topic: Dishonour of cheques for insufficiency of funds (Sections 138 to 140)
mcq.fast: Complaint = within 1 month of the cause of action.

mcq.q: Under Section 139, the court presumes, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder received the cheque:
options: As a gift
As a security deposit only
By mistake
In discharge of a debt or other liability, wholly or in part
mcq.explain: Section 139 lets the court assume, until the drawer proves otherwise, that the holder got the cheque to settle all or part of a debt or liability. The burden shifts to the drawer to rebut this presumption with evidence.
mcq.topic: Dishonour of cheques for insufficiency of funds (Sections 138 to 140)
mcq.fast: Presumption favours the HOLDER: cheque was for a debt.

mcq.q: A bill of exchange dated 15 January 2026 is payable two months after date. Its date of maturity (no holidays involved) is:
options: 15 March 2026
17 March 2026
18 March 2026
15 April 2026
mcq.explain: Under Sections 22 and 23, an instrument payable a stated number of months after date falls due on the corresponding day of the month, plus three days of grace. Two months after 15 January is 15 March; adding three days of grace gives 18 March 2026, which is not a holiday here.
mcq.topic: Meaning and characteristics of negotiable instruments (Section 13)
mcq.fast: Months after date -> same date + 3 days of grace.

mcq.q: The wording of an instrument allows it to be read as a note or as a bill. Under Section 17 the holder:
options: Must treat it as a promissory note
May treat it as either, at his choice; once chosen, it is treated as such thereafter
Must treat it as a bill of exchange
Cannot enforce it, as it is void for ambiguity
mcq.explain: Section 17 deals with ambiguous instruments: if the wording allows the paper to be read as a note or as a bill, the holder picks one, and from then on it is dealt with as the one he picked. Ambiguity does not make it void.
mcq.fast: Ambiguous instrument = holder's choice (s.17).

mcq.q: Amit signs a stamped blank instrument and gives it to Bimal, authorising him to fill in an amount. Bimal fills in ₹50,000 and negotiates it to a holder in due course. Under Section 20, Amit is liable to the holder in due course for:
options: Nothing, as the instrument was blank
Only the amount he actually intended
The amount filled in, up to the value the stamp covers
Twice the amount filled in
mcq.explain: Section 20 deals with inchoate stamped instruments. Signing and handing over a stamped but blank or incomplete paper gives the holder apparent authority to fill it in for any sum up to the value the stamp covers. He is liable to a holder in due course for the amount filled in within that limit.
mcq.fast: Inchoate stamped instrument: signer liable up to the stamp value to a holder in due course.

mcq.q: A cheque crossed generally (two parallel transverse lines, with or without "& Co.") can be paid by the bank:
options: Only in cash at the counter
Only to a banker, i.e. through a bank account
To any person presenting it
Only to the drawer
mcq.explain: A general crossing, under Sections 123 and 126, directs the paying banker to pay the cheque only to a banker. The money must be collected through a bank account, which makes it traceable and protects against wrongful encashment. A special crossing names a particular banker.
mcq.fast: Crossed = through a bank, never over the counter.

mcq.q: A cheque crossed "Not Negotiable" is transferred. The transferee:
options: Cannot transfer it at all
Gets no better title than the transferor had — Section 130
Becomes a holder in due course automatically
Can encash it at the counter
mcq.explain: Section 130 provides that a person taking a cheque crossed generally or specially and bearing the words "not negotiable" does not have, and cannot give, a better title than that of the person from whom he took it. The cheque remains transferable, but the special protection of a holder in due course is lost.
mcq.fast: "Not negotiable" ≠ not transferable; it only removes better-title protection.

mcq.q: A material alteration made in a negotiable instrument without the consent of the parties liable on it:
options: Has no effect at all
Renders it void as against anyone who was a party before the alteration and did not consent — Section 87
Makes it valid for the altered amount against everyone
Converts it into an ambiguous instrument
mcq.explain: Section 87 provides that any material alteration of a negotiable instrument renders it void as against anyone who is a party to it at the time of the alteration and does not consent to it, unless the alteration was made to carry out the common intention of the original parties. Changing the amount or date is material.
mcq.topic: Meaning and characteristics of negotiable instruments (Section 13)
mcq.fast: Unauthorised material alteration = void against non-consenting earlier parties.

mcq.q: An instrument drawn in India on a person resident in India and payable in India is:
options: A foreign instrument
An inland instrument — Section 11
An inchoate instrument
An ambiguous instrument
mcq.explain: Section 11 treats an instrument as inland if it is made in India and is either payable in India or drawn on someone living in India. Any instrument that is not inland is a foreign instrument under Section 12. Here all three links are in India.
mcq.fast: Made in India + payable/drawee in India = inland.

mcq.q: A bill expressed to be payable "at sight" is, under Section 21, payable:
options: Three months after sight
On demand
On the date of maturity plus three days of grace
Only after acceptance by a notary
mcq.explain: Section 21 states that in a promissory note or bill, the expressions "at sight" and "on presentment" mean on demand. Days of grace apply only to instruments payable otherwise than on demand. A bill payable "after sight" is different; it must first be presented for acceptance.
mcq.fast: "At sight" = "on presentment" = on demand.

mcq.q: Under Section 143A, in a complaint under Section 138, the court may order the drawer to pay interim compensation to the complainant not exceeding:
options: 50% of the amount of the cheque
10% of the amount of the cheque
20% of the amount of the cheque
The full amount of the cheque
mcq.explain: Section 143A, inserted in 2018, allows the trial court to order the drawer to pay interim compensation of up to 20% of the cheque amount, in a summary trial or summons case where the drawer pleads not guilty, and in other cases on framing of charge. It is to be paid within 60 days, extendable by 30 days.
mcq.topic: Dishonour of cheques for insufficiency of funds (Sections 138 to 140)
mcq.fast: Interim compensation = up to 20% (s.143A).

mcq.q: Which statement about an offence under Section 138 is correct?
options: It can never be settled once a complaint is filed
It is compoundable — the parties may settle it under Section 147
It is triable only by a High Court
It is a civil wrong with no punishment
mcq.explain: Section 147 makes every offence punishable under the Negotiable Instruments Act compoundable, notwithstanding the Code of Criminal Procedure. The drawer and payee can therefore settle a cheque-bounce case. Such cases are tried by a Metropolitan Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate of the first class under Section 142.
mcq.topic: Dishonour of cheques for insufficiency of funds (Sections 138 to 140)
mcq.fast: Cheque bounce = criminal but compoundable (s.147).

mcq.q: Under Section 138, a cheque must be presented to the bank within six months of its date or within its period of validity, whichever is earlier. As the RBI has fixed the validity of cheques at three months, the effective period is:
options: Three months from the date of the cheque
Six months from the date of the cheque
One month from the date of the cheque
One year from the date of the cheque
mcq.explain: Clause (a) of the proviso to Section 138 requires presentment within six months from the date on which the cheque is drawn or within its validity period, whichever is earlier. Since the RBI reduced the validity of cheques to three months from 1 April 2012, a cheque must in practice be presented within three months.
mcq.fast: Earlier of 6 months and validity (3 months) = 3 months.

mcq.q: Which is NOT a characteristic of a negotiable instrument?
options: It is freely transferable by delivery or indorsement and delivery
The holder can sue in his own name
A transferee can never get a better title than the transferor
Certain presumptions, such as consideration, apply in favour of the holder
mcq.explain: Negotiable instruments are freely transferable, the holder can sue in his own name, and Section 118 raises presumptions such as consideration. Their key feature is that a holder in due course gets a good title even if the transferor's title was defective. Saying the transferee can never get a better title describes ordinary property, not negotiability.
mcq.topic: Meaning and characteristics of negotiable instruments (Section 13)
mcq.fast: Negotiability = better title for a holder in due course. The "never better title" option is the odd one out.

mcq.q: A drawee who accepts a bill of exchange signs his assent on it. Before acceptance, the drawee:
options: Is liable as the principal debtor
Is liable as a surety
Is not liable on the bill
Is liable only for interest
mcq.explain: A bill of exchange is an order addressed to the drawee. He becomes liable on it only when he accepts it by signing his assent; he is then called the acceptor and becomes primarily liable. Until acceptance, the drawee owes nothing on the bill, though the drawer remains liable to the payee if it is dishonoured.
mcq.fast: Drawee is bound only after accepting.

mcq.q: Three days of grace are added in computing the maturity of:
options: A cheque
A bill of exchange payable at sight
A bill of exchange payable 90 days after date
A promissory note payable on demand
mcq.explain: Section 22 gives three extra days of grace to notes and bills that are payable at a future time; such an instrument matures three days after its stated due date. Instruments payable on demand, at sight or on presentment get no grace. A cheque is always payable on demand, so no days of grace apply to it.
mcq.fast: Days of grace only for time instruments — never for on-demand ones like cheques.

mcq.q: The drawer of a bill names, in addition to the drawee, a person to whom the holder may go if the bill is dishonoured. That person is called:
options: An acceptor for honour
A holder in due course
A drawee in case of need — Section 7
An indorsee
mcq.explain: Section 7 calls a person named in the bill, or in an indorsement on it, as a fallback to the drawee a "drawee in case of need". The holder may present the bill to him if the drawee does not accept or pay.
mcq.fast: Back-up drawee named on the bill = drawee in case of need.

mcq.q: Until the contrary is proved, Section 118 presumes that every negotiable instrument:
options: Was given as a gift
Was made or drawn for consideration
Was obtained by fraud
Was transferred after maturity
mcq.explain: Section 118 raises several presumptions in favour of the holder unless the contrary is proved: that the instrument was made or drawn for consideration, that it bears the date on which it was made, that it was transferred before maturity, that indorsements were made in the order they appear, and that the holder is a holder in due course.
mcq.topic: Meaning and characteristics of negotiable instruments (Section 13)
mcq.fast: Section 118 presumptions all favour the holder: consideration, date, before maturity, due course.
